opus-5.5.text:
I think the main constraint really comes down to the support polygon. When you have a small platform, like a quadruped with a relatively compact base or a robot standing on a narrow footprint, the area within which you can keep your center of mass stable is quite limited. So any time you move the torso, whether you're leaning to reach for something, shifting your weight, or trying to manipulate an object with an arm mounted on top, you're shifting the center of mass, and you very quickly run up against the edge of that stable region.

On top of that, there are dynamic effects. It's not just where the center of mass sits statically; if you move the torso quickly, you generate inertial forces that the legs have to compensate for. With a small base, you have less leverage to counteract those forces, so the robot can tip over even if the final pose would have been statically fine.

Then there are the hardware limits themselves: joint ranges, torque limits in the legs, and the kinematics of how far the body can actually tilt or translate relative to the feet. On a compact robot, those ranges are often tighter, so even if balance weren't an issue, you just can't move the body very far.

What's been interesting in our work with reinforcement learning is that, rather than hand-designing all these constraints, you can let the policy learn where those limits are through training in simulation. The robot discovers how far it can lean, how fast it can shift its weight, and it can even learn to step or reposition its feet to enlarge the support region when it needs more reach. That turns what used to be a hard constraint into something the controller can actively work around, which is a big part of why these learned controllers look so much more agile than classical approaches.

r001.rationale: The response explains that torso movement shifts the center of mass toward the edge of the limited stable region, where the robot can tip over.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that comes up a lot when people look at our humanoid work and ask why the upper body isn't doing more. The fundamental issue is really the support polygon. If you have a small platform, meaning a small footprint, the feet are close together and relatively small, then the region where your center of mass projection has to stay in order to remain statically stable is tiny. Every time you move the torso, you shift the center of mass, and with a small base you run out of margin almost immediately.

So the constraint isn't really the torso joints themselves. The arms, the waist, the spine, those can move quite fast. The constraint is that any torso motion has to be compensated by the legs, either by shifting the feet or by generating the right ground reaction forces, and the legs have limited authority. There's only so much torque the ankles can produce, and once the center of pressure reaches the edge of the foot, you're done, you have to step or you fall.

What this means in practice is that torso motion and locomotion become fully coupled. You can't treat the upper body as a separate manipulation system sitting on top of a mobile base, the way you could with a wheeled platform that has a wide stance. Every reach, every lean, has to be planned together with the footsteps. That's actually one of the reasons we moved toward learning whole-body policies rather than decomposing the problem. If you train a single policy that sees the full state and controls everything, it learns to use the legs to create room for the torso to move. It'll take a small step, or shift weight preemptively, before the arm swings out. A modular controller tends to struggle there because the upper-body controller doesn't know what the lower-body controller can afford.

The other thing I'd add is that it's partly a dynamic versus static question. If you're willing to be dynamically stable rather than statically stable, you can actually get away with a lot more torso motion on a small platform, because you use momentum. Humans do this constantly. But that requires a controller that's comfortable operating far from equilibrium, and that's where simulation-based reinforcement learning has really helped us, because the policy has seen millions of those situations and recovered from them.

r001.rationale: It explains that torso movement shifts the center of mass and that, with a small support base, the robot can run out of stability margin and fall.

astra-6.text: With a small support platform, you have less room to shift your center of mass before you lose balance. So torso motion is coupled to what the legs are doing. If you lean too far, you need to compensate with the rest of the body or take a step. The constraint is really maintaining balance while making that movement.

r001.rationale: It says that leaning too far means the robot must compensate or step, and identifies maintaining balance as the constraint on a small platform, clearly conveying the risk of toppling.

sol-6.1.text: The main constraint is balance. With a small support area, you can’t move the torso very far without shifting the center of mass outside that area. So the torso motion has to be coordinated with the legs—you need to shift your weight or take a step to compensate. It’s not just about how much range of motion the joints have; it’s about whether the whole robot can remain stable while using it.

r001.rationale: The response says that moving the torso too far can shift the center of mass outside the small support area and make the robot unstable, which communicates the risk of toppling.
